claims.claim: Holtzman and colleagues report that the per-token probabilities the model assigns to human-written continuations vary far more from step to step than those of beam-search text given the same context.
claims.source: Ari Holtzman, Jan Buys, Li Du, Maxwell Forbes and Yejin Choi, 'The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration', ICLR 2020 (arXiv v2, 14 Feb 2020)
claims.quote: increased variance that characterizes human text
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 Large (762M) generating continuations of held-out WebText documents; measurement published February 2020; register measured: web-scraped documents (news/review prose), not fiction or archival record.

claims.claim: Holtzman and colleagues assert that human language does not stay in a high-probability zone across consecutive tokens but veers into lower-probability, more informative ones.
claims.source: Ari Holtzman, Jan Buys, Li Du, Maxwell Forbes and Yejin Choi, 'The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration', ICLR 2020 (arXiv v2, 14 Feb 2020)
claims.quote: Natural language rarely remains in a high probability zone
claims.page: section 4.3, 'Natural Language Does Not Maximize Probability'
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 Large (762M) scoring held-out WebText, February 2020; register measured: web-scraped documents.

claims.claim: Holtzman and colleagues report that a language model raises the probability of a phrase each time that phrase repeats, so repetition is self-reinforcing.
claims.source: Ari Holtzman, Jan Buys, Li Du, Maxwell Forbes and Yejin Choi, 'The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration', ICLR 2020 (arXiv v2, 14 Feb 2020)
claims.quote: The probability of a repeated phrase increases with each repetition
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 Large (762M), February 2020; the effect held 'for the vast majority of phrases we tested, regardless of phrase length'; register measured: WebText continuations.

claims.claim: Holtzman and colleagues conjecture that models trained on a per-word likelihood objective are pushed toward the lowest common denominator rather than toward informative language, so larger models alone will not cure blandness.
claims.source: Ari Holtzman, Jan Buys, Li Du, Maxwell Forbes and Yejin Choi, 'The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration', ICLR 2020 (arXiv v2, 14 Feb 2020)
claims.quote: forced to favor the lowest common denominator, rather than informative language
claims.modelEra: argued about likelihood-trained language models generally, from GPT-2 Large observations, February 2020.

claims.claim: Holtzman and colleagues ground their conjecture in Grice's maxims, saying that people avoid stating the obvious and therefore disfavour maximally predictable wording.
claims.source: Ari Holtzman, Jan Buys, Li Du, Maxwell Forbes and Yejin Choi, 'The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration', ICLR 2020 (arXiv v2, 14 Feb 2020)
claims.quote: people optimize against stating the obvious
claims.modelEra: theoretical claim about human language, offered February 2020 alongside GPT-2 Large measurements.

claims.claim: Holtzman and colleagues measured that sampling temperatures below 0.9 sharply increase repetition in GPT-2 Large generations.
claims.source: Ari Holtzman, Jan Buys, Li Du, Maxwell Forbes and Yejin Choi, 'The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration', ICLR 2020 (arXiv v2, 14 Feb 2020)
claims.quote: Sampling with temperatures lower than 0.9 severely increase repetition
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 Large (762M), February 2020; repetition scored as a phrase of at least two tokens repeating three or more times at the end of a 200-token generation; register measured: WebText continuations.

claims.claim: In Holtzman and colleagues' Table 1, greedy decoding from GPT-2 Large produced a repetition rate of 73.66 percent against 0.28 percent for the human reference text.
claims.source: Ari Holtzman, Jan Buys, Li Du, Maxwell Forbes and Yejin Choi, 'The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration', ICLR 2020 (arXiv v2, 14 Feb 2020)
claims.page: Table 1 (columns Repetition %, rows Human and Greedy)
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 Large (762M), 5,000 generated passages of up to 200 tokens, February 2020; register measured: WebText continuations.

claims.claim: In Holtzman and colleagues' Table 1, beam search with width 16 gave generated text a perplexity of 1.48 against 12.38 for human text under the same model.
claims.source: Ari Holtzman, Jan Buys, Li Du, Maxwell Forbes and Yejin Choi, 'The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration', ICLR 2020 (arXiv v2, 14 Feb 2020)
claims.page: Table 1 (columns Perplexity, rows Human and Beam b=16)
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 Large (762M), February 2020; register measured: WebText continuations.

claims.claim: Holtzman and colleagues report that pure sampling produced text of higher perplexity than the human reference, which they read as the model confusing itself by sampling too many unlikely tokens.
claims.source: Ari Holtzman, Jan Buys, Li Du, Maxwell Forbes and Yejin Choi, 'The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration', ICLR 2020 (arXiv v2, 14 Feb 2020)
claims.quote: the model is confusing itself: sampling too many unlikely tokens
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 Large (762M), February 2020; pure sampling perplexity 22.73 against human 12.38; register measured: WebText continuations.

claims.claim: Holtzman and colleagues' degeneration findings were measured on a single model, GPT-2 Large at 762 million parameters.
claims.source: Ari Holtzman, Jan Buys, Li Du, Maxwell Forbes and Yejin Choi, 'The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration', ICLR 2020 (arXiv v2, 14 Feb 2020)
claims.quote: We perform experiments using the Large model (762M parameters)
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 Large, 762M parameters, experiments run 2019, published February 2020; register measured: WebText continuations. No instruction-tuned or RLHF model was in scope.

claims.claim: Meister and colleagues explain the rising probability of a repeated substring by saying the substring carries less information with each further occurrence.
claims.source: Clara Meister, Tiago Pimentel, Gian Wiher and Ryan Cotterell, 'Locally Typical Sampling', TACL 2023 (arXiv v6, 5 Jun 2025)
claims.quote: the substring conveys less and less information after each occurrence
claims.modelEra: information-theoretic explanation offered for the effect Holtzman and colleagues measured on GPT-2; the paper's own experiments used GPT-2 medium and large and BART, 2022-2023.

claims.claim: Meister and colleagues argue that high-probability text reads as dull because low probability is low information content, so probable text is literally uninformative.
claims.source: Clara Meister, Tiago Pimentel, Gian Wiher and Ryan Cotterell, 'Locally Typical Sampling', TACL 2023 (arXiv v6, 5 Jun 2025)
claims.quote: its low information content likely makes for boring
claims.modelEra: information-theoretic argument about probabilistic language generators generally, 2022-2023.

claims.claim: Meister and colleagues measured that in human reference text each word's information content sits close to the model's conditional entropy at that step, a per-token deviation distribution peaked near zero.
claims.source: Clara Meister, Tiago Pimentel, Gian Wiher and Ryan Cotterell, 'Locally Typical Sampling', TACL 2023 (arXiv v6, 5 Jun 2025)
claims.quote: human language indeed tends to have per-word information content quite close
claims.modelEra: probabilities and entropies from GPT-2 medium finetuned on WikiText-103, plus WritingPrompts and CNN/DailyMail models, 2022; registers measured: encyclopedic (WikiText-103), story (WritingPrompts) and news (CNN/DailyMail). NOTE: this is deviation from the step-wise conditional entropy, not raw surprisal, so it qualifies rather than contradicts Holtzman's burstiness finding.

claims.claim: Meister and colleagues found that their repetition metric was much less sensitive to the typical-sampling parameter tau than to top-k's k or nucleus's eta.
claims.source: Clara Meister, Tiago Pimentel, Gian Wiher and Ryan Cotterell, 'Locally Typical Sampling', TACL 2023 (arXiv v6, 5 Jun 2025)
claims.quote: REP appears to be far less sensitive to
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 large finetuned on WritingPrompts, 2022; register measured: short prompted stories.

claims.claim: In Meister and colleagues' Table 1 for story generation, human reference text scored a REP of 0.28 while nucleus sampling at eta 0.9 and top-k at k 30 both scored 0.35.
claims.source: Clara Meister, Tiago Pimentel, Gian Wiher and Ryan Cotterell, 'Locally Typical Sampling', TACL 2023 (arXiv v6, 5 Jun 2025)
claims.page: Table 1 (WritingPrompts, column REP, rows Reference, Nucleus eta=0.9, Top-k k=30)
claims.modelEra: finetuned GPT-2 large on the WritingPrompts test set, 2022; register measured: prompted short fiction.

claims.claim: Meister and colleagues concede that every decoding strategy they tested scored close to the human reference in their human ratings, in some cases above it.
claims.source: Clara Meister, Tiago Pimentel, Gian Wiher and Ryan Cotterell, 'Locally Typical Sampling', TACL 2023 (arXiv v6, 5 Jun 2025)
claims.quote: all the strategies we explore are quite close to human-level performance
claims.modelEra: Amazon Mechanical Turk raters on GPT-2 large WritingPrompts stories and BART CNN/DailyMail summaries, 2022; human reference scored 4.12 and several decoders scored 4.13 to 4.15 on the averaged five-point scale.

claims.claim: Meister and colleagues state that both maximisation-based and stochastic decoding strategies eventually fall into repetitive loops.
claims.source: Clara Meister, Tiago Pimentel, Gian Wiher and Ryan Cotterell, 'Locally Typical Sampling', TACL 2023 (arXiv v6, 5 Jun 2025)
claims.quote: Both types of strategies tend to eventually fall into repetitive loops
claims.modelEra: claim about probabilistic language generators as of 2022; their own experiments used GPT-2 medium and large and BART.

claims.claim: Nguyen and colleagues claim that under min-p sampling temperatures of 2 or 3 increase diversity with much less loss of coherence than existing methods suffer.
claims.source: Nguyen Nhat Minh, Andrew Baker, Clement Neo, Allen Roush, Andreas Kirsch and Ravid Shwartz-Ziv, 'Turning Up the Heat: Min-p Sampling for Creative and Coherent LLM Outputs', ICLR 2025 (arXiv v8, 20 Nov 2025)
claims.quote: enhancing diversity with much lower loss of coherence
claims.page: section 4, Parameter Selection Guidelines, Temperature Settings
claims.modelEra: Mistral 7B, Mistral Large, Llama 3 70B and openchat-3.5-0106, benchmarks run 2024-2025; registers measured: reasoning benchmarks (GPQA, GSM8K) and prompted creative writing (AlpacaEval Creative Writing).

claims.claim: Nguyen and colleagues assert that top-p sampling struggles at higher temperatures, where it produces incoherent or repetitive output.
claims.source: Nguyen Nhat Minh, Andrew Baker, Clement Neo, Allen Roush, Andreas Kirsch and Ravid Shwartz-Ziv, 'Turning Up the Heat: Min-p Sampling for Creative and Coherent LLM Outputs', ICLR 2025 (arXiv v8, 20 Nov 2025)
claims.quote: especially at higher temperatures which lead to incoherent or repetitive outputs
claims.modelEra: claim about top-p on Mistral and Llama 3 family models, 2024-2025.

claims.claim: In Nguyen and colleagues' human evaluation at temperature 3 with the lower-diversity setting, min-p stories scored 7.74 out of 10 for quality against 5.75 for top-p and 6.75 for standard sampling.
claims.source: Nguyen Nhat Minh, Andrew Baker, Clement Neo, Allen Roush, Andreas Kirsch and Ravid Shwartz-Ziv, 'Turning Up the Heat: Min-p Sampling for Creative and Coherent LLM Outputs', ICLR 2025 (arXiv v8, 20 Nov 2025)
claims.page: Table 4 (row T=3, Quality, Lower Diversity Settings)
claims.modelEra: Llama 3 70B answering the prompt 'Write me a creative story?', rated 1-10 by Prolific participants screened as regular LLM users, 2024-2025; register measured: prompted short fiction.

claims.claim: Nguyen and colleagues report min-p winning 56.54 percent on the AlpacaEval Creative Writing benchmark at temperature 1.5, against 53.18 percent for temperature-only sampling.
claims.source: Nguyen Nhat Minh, Andrew Baker, Clement Neo, Allen Roush, Andreas Kirsch and Ravid Shwartz-Ziv, 'Turning Up the Heat: Min-p Sampling for Creative and Coherent LLM Outputs', ICLR 2025 (arXiv v8, 20 Nov 2025)
claims.page: Table 3b (AlpacaEval Creative Writing % win, column tau=1.5)
claims.modelEra: openchat-3.5-0106 generating, GPT-4 Turbo as judge, 2024; register measured: prompted creative writing. This is an LLM-as-judge score, not a human one.

claims.claim: Nguyen and colleagues concede that their human evaluation rests on a limited sample size and gives directional insight rather than a settled result.
claims.source: Nguyen Nhat Minh, Andrew Baker, Clement Neo, Allen Roush, Andreas Kirsch and Ravid Shwartz-Ziv, 'Turning Up the Heat: Min-p Sampling for Creative and Coherent LLM Outputs', ICLR 2025 (arXiv v8, 20 Nov 2025)
claims.quote: this represents a limited sample size, it provides valuable directional insights
claims.modelEra: their own Llama 3 70B human study, 2024-2025; each configuration was three samples rated as a triplet, a point estimate of diversity.

claims.claim: Nguyen and colleagues relay, from Ilya Gusev's run of Sam Paech's EQ-Bench Creative Writing benchmark, a min-p score of 62 at temperature 1.5 against the baseline's 51.5 at temperature 1.0.
claims.source: Nguyen Nhat Minh, Andrew Baker, Clement Neo, Allen Roush, Andreas Kirsch and Ravid Shwartz-Ziv, 'Turning Up the Heat: Min-p Sampling for Creative and Coherent LLM Outputs', ICLR 2025 (arXiv v8, 20 Nov 2025)
claims.modelEra: a third-party benchmark run reported inside the min-p paper, dated 2024; benchmark authored by Sam Paech, run by Ilya Gusev on Reddit. RELAY: the primary was not fetched here.

claims.claim: Basu and colleagues measured that the percentage of repeated tokens falls as the observed cross-entropy of the generated text rises.
claims.source: Sourya Basu, Govardana Sachitanandam Ramachandran, Nitish Shirish Keskar and Lav R. Varshney, 'Mirostat: A Neural Text Decoding Algorithm that Directly Controls Perplexity', ICLR 2021 (arXiv v2, 14 Jan 2021)
claims.quote: percentage repetition decreases with increase in cross-entropy
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 117M generating 200-token continuations from a fixed context, published January 2021; register measured: open-ended continuation of a web-text context.

claims.claim: Basu and colleagues found that for a fixed GPT-2 model the relation between repetition and observed cross-entropy does not depend on which sampling method produced the text.
claims.source: Sourya Basu, Govardana Sachitanandam Ramachandran, Nitish Shirish Keskar and Lav R. Varshney, 'Mirostat: A Neural Text Decoding Algorithm that Directly Controls Perplexity', ICLR 2021 (arXiv v2, 14 Jan 2021)
claims.quote: this relation is independent of the sampling method
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 117M with top-k, top-p, temperature and mirostat sampling, January 2021; register measured: open-ended continuation. This is the strongest mechanism claim in the roster: the sampler is not the variable, the entropy of the sampled text is.

claims.claim: Basu and colleagues measured that sentence-level repetition in GPT-2 output effectively disappears above an observed cross-entropy of about 2.5.
claims.source: Sourya Basu, Govardana Sachitanandam Ramachandran, Nitish Shirish Keskar and Lav R. Varshney, 'Mirostat: A Neural Text Decoding Algorithm that Directly Controls Perplexity', ICLR 2021 (arXiv v2, 14 Jan 2021)
claims.quote: beyond a threshold of cross-entropy, which seems to be around 2.5
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 117M, January 2021; measured as n-gram repetition for larger n; the paper notes word-level (1-gram) repetition persists above that threshold and should, because human text repeats pronouns and conjunctions.

claims.claim: Basu and colleagues measured that human-written continuation settles at a limiting cross-entropy rate as it lengthens, falling into neither the boredom nor the confusion trap.
claims.source: Sourya Basu, Govardana Sachitanandam Ramachandran, Nitish Shirish Keskar and Lav R. Varshney, 'Mirostat: A Neural Text Decoding Algorithm that Directly Controls Perplexity', ICLR 2021 (arXiv v2, 14 Jan 2021)
claims.quote: Human-generated text converges to some limiting value of cross-
claims.page: section 5.3, Boredom and Confusion Traps, discussion of Figure 5c
claims.modelEra: single-sample human continuation scored against GPT-2 117M over 900 tokens, January 2021; register measured: the human corpus text following a fixed web context. The quotation breaks at a line-wrapped hyphen in the fetched PDF text; the word completed is 'cross-entropy'.

claims.claim: Basu and colleagues report that at a target cross-entropy of 3 more than half their raters guessed the AI-generated text was human-written.
claims.source: Sourya Basu, Govardana Sachitanandam Ramachandran, Nitish Shirish Keskar and Lav R. Varshney, 'Mirostat: A Neural Text Decoding Algorithm that Directly Controls Perplexity', ICLR 2021 (arXiv v2, 14 Jan 2021)
claims.quote: more than half of raters mistakenly guessed the AI-generated text
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 (117M) 300-token generations rated by 43 participants from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and IIT Kanpur, on 1-7 Likert scales, January 2021; register measured: open-ended continuation.

claims.claim: Basu and colleagues measured that GPT-2-XL at 1558 million parameters repeats slightly less than GPT-2 at 117 million parameters at the same observed cross-entropy.
claims.source: Sourya Basu, Govardana Sachitanandam Ramachandran, Nitish Shirish Keskar and Lav R. Varshney, 'Mirostat: A Neural Text Decoding Algorithm that Directly Controls Perplexity', ICLR 2021 (arXiv v2, 14 Jan 2021)
claims.quote: have slightly less repetitions for a fixed value of cross-entropy
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 117M through GPT-2-XL 1558M under top-p sampling, January 2021; register measured: open-ended continuation. Scale reduces the tell only slightly once entropy is held fixed.

claims.claim: Basu and colleagues name the low-cross-entropy failure of small k and p values the boredom trap, in which repetition grows as the generated text lengthens.
claims.source: Sourya Basu, Govardana Sachitanandam Ramachandran, Nitish Shirish Keskar and Lav R. Varshney, 'Mirostat: A Neural Text Decoding Algorithm that Directly Controls Perplexity', ICLR 2021 (arXiv v2, 14 Jan 2021)
claims.quote: leads to excessive repetitions
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 117M over 900-token generations, January 2021; register measured: open-ended continuation.

claims.claim: Su and colleagues argue that degeneration originates in the anisotropic distribution of a language model's token representations rather than in the decoding rule alone.
claims.source: Yixuan Su, Tian Lan, Yan Wang, Dani Yogatama, Lingpeng Kong and Nigel Collier, 'A Contrastive Framework for Neural Text Generation', NeurIPS 2022 (arXiv v3, 26 Sep 2022)
claims.quote: stems from the anisotropic distribution of token representations
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 and finetuned GPT-2 large, 2022; register measured: Wikitext-103 (encyclopedic prose).

claims.claim: Su and colleagues measured cosine similarities above 0.95 between the representations of different tokens within a single sentence in GPT-2.
claims.source: Yixuan Su, Tian Lan, Yan Wang, Dani Yogatama, Lingpeng Kong and Nigel Collier, 'A Contrastive Framework for Neural Text Generation', NeurIPS 2022 (arXiv v3, 26 Sep 2022)
claims.quote: the cosine similarities between tokens within a sentence are over 0.95
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 output layer representations, 2022; register measured: Wikitext-103 sentences.

claims.claim: Su and colleagues ran their whole degeneration evaluation on the Wikitext-103 test set, that is on encyclopedic prose.
claims.source: Yixuan Su, Tian Lan, Yan Wang, Dani Yogatama, Lingpeng Kong and Nigel Collier, 'A Contrastive Framework for Neural Text Generation', NeurIPS 2022 (arXiv v3, 26 Sep 2022)
claims.page: Table 1 caption: 'Evaluation results on Wikitext-103 test set'
claims.modelEra: MLE, unlikelihood-trained and SimCTG GPT-2 models, 2022; register measured: Wikipedia article prose, the closest register in this roster to an archival or gazetteer record.

claims.claim: In Su and colleagues' Wikitext-103 table, greedy decoding from the MLE model scored a rep-2 of 69.21 against 3.92 for the human reference.
claims.source: Yixuan Su, Tian Lan, Yan Wang, Dani Yogatama, Lingpeng Kong and Nigel Collier, 'A Contrastive Framework for Neural Text Generation', NeurIPS 2022 (arXiv v3, 26 Sep 2022)
claims.page: Table 1 (column rep-2, rows MLE greedy and Human)
claims.modelEra: GPT-2 finetuned with MLE on Wikitext-103, 2022; register measured: encyclopedic prose.

claims.claim: In Su and colleagues' Wikitext-103 table, nucleus sampling produced text with a generation perplexity of 47.19 against 24.01 for the human reference, so the sampled text was less predictable than the human original rather than flatter.
claims.source: Yixuan Su, Tian Lan, Yan Wang, Dani Yogatama, Lingpeng Kong and Nigel Collier, 'A Contrastive Framework for Neural Text Generation', NeurIPS 2022 (arXiv v3, 26 Sep 2022)
claims.page: Table 1 (column gen-ppl, rows SimCTG nucleus and Human)
claims.modelEra: SimCTG-finetuned GPT-2 on Wikitext-103 with nucleus p=0.95, 2022; register measured: encyclopedic prose. This cuts against a blanket claim that machine text is always the low-entropy side of the comparison.

claims.claim: Su and colleagues' human evaluation covered 200 Wikitext-103 prefixes scored by five graders, producing 9,000 annotated samples.
claims.source: Yixuan Su, Tian Lan, Yan Wang, Dani Yogatama, Lingpeng Kong and Nigel Collier, 'A Contrastive Framework for Neural Text Generation', NeurIPS 2022 (arXiv v3, 26 Sep 2022)
claims.quote: results in 9,000 annotated samples in total
claims.modelEra: MLE, unlikelihood and SimCTG GPT-2 models plus SimCTG-large, continuations of length 128 from 32-token prefixes, five-point Likert on coherence, fluency and informativeness, 2022; register measured: encyclopedic prose.

claims.claim: Schaeffer, Kazdan and Denisov-Blanch re-analysed the min-p paper's own human-evaluation data and concluded min-p did not outperform baseline samplers on quality.
claims.source: Rylan Schaeffer, Joshua Kazdan and Yegor Denisov-Blanch (Stanford University), 'Min-p, Max Exaggeration: A Critical Analysis of Min-p Sampling in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 19 Jun 2025
claims.quote: our reanalysis demonstrates min-p did not out
claims.page: Abstract (the quotation breaks at a line-wrapped hyphen; the word completed is 'outperform')
claims.modelEra: re-analysis of Nguyen and colleagues' 2024 Llama 3 70B creative-story human study, published June 2025; register measured: prompted short fiction.

claims.claim: Schaeffer and colleagues report that in the min-p paper's own human-evaluation data the three samplers scored similarly on both quality and diversity, with 95 percent confidence intervals frequently overlapping.
claims.source: Rylan Schaeffer, Joshua Kazdan and Yegor Denisov-Blanch (Stanford University), 'Min-p, Max Exaggeration: A Critical Analysis of Min-p Sampling in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 19 Jun 2025
claims.quote: the three samplers provide similar quality and similar diversity
claims.modelEra: Nguyen and colleagues' 2024 Llama 3 70B Prolific study, re-plotted June 2025; register measured: prompted short fiction.

claims.claim: Schaeffer and colleagues' twelve one-sided paired t-tests on the min-p paper's data supported min-p's superiority in one of twelve comparisons after Bonferroni correction at alpha 0.05.
claims.source: Rylan Schaeffer, Joshua Kazdan and Yegor Denisov-Blanch (Stanford University), 'Min-p, Max Exaggeration: A Critical Analysis of Min-p Sampling in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 19 Jun 2025
claims.modelEra: re-analysis of the 2024 min-p human study, June 2025; paired t-tests with 52 degrees of freedom; without correction 5 of 12 reached alpha 0.05.

claims.claim: Schaeffer and colleagues, annotating the min-p study's free-text responses, found that more human evaluators explicitly preferred plain temperature sampling than preferred min-p.
claims.source: Rylan Schaeffer, Joshua Kazdan and Yegor Denisov-Blanch (Stanford University), 'Min-p, Max Exaggeration: A Critical Analysis of Min-p Sampling in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 19 Jun 2025
claims.quote: more human evaluators explicitly preferred basic sampling than preferred min-p
claims.modelEra: qualitative responses from Nguyen and colleagues' 2024 Prolific study, re-annotated June 2025; register measured: prompted short fiction.

claims.claim: Schaeffer and colleagues report that the min-p paper's creative-writing table gave the higher of two available scores for min-p and the lower of two for top-p.
claims.source: Rylan Schaeffer, Joshua Kazdan and Yegor Denisov-Blanch (Stanford University), 'Min-p, Max Exaggeration: A Critical Analysis of Min-p Sampling in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 19 Jun 2025
claims.quote: the higher of two scores was reported for min-p
claims.modelEra: audit of the min-p paper's AlpacaEval Creative Writing table, June 2025; the reported min-p win rate of 52.01 corresponds to p=0.05 while p=0.01 yields 50.14.

claims.claim: Schaeffer and colleagues conclude that all the samplers they swept perform roughly the same once each is given the same amount of hyperparameter tuning.
claims.source: Rylan Schaeffer, Joshua Kazdan and Yegor Denisov-Blanch (Stanford University), 'Min-p, Max Exaggeration: A Critical Analysis of Min-p Sampling in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 19 Jun 2025
claims.quote: all samplers perform roughly the same once given the same
claims.page: section 6, Discussion and Limitations, Scientific Conclusions
claims.modelEra: 9 models (Qwen 2.5 0.5B-7B, Mistral 7B v0.1, Llama 3.1 8B and 3.2 3B, Gemma 2 2B and 9B), base and instruct, 4 samplers, 31 temperatures from 0.0 to 3.0, swept June 2025; register measured: GSM8K chain-of-thought, a reasoning task, not prose.

claims.claim: Schaeffer and colleagues allow that min-p may sometimes help at higher temperatures, with the caveat that absolute performance in that regime is meaningfully worse than at standard temperatures.
claims.source: Rylan Schaeffer, Joshua Kazdan and Yegor Denisov-Blanch (Stanford University), 'Min-p, Max Exaggeration: A Critical Analysis of Min-p Sampling in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 19 Jun 2025
claims.quote: min-p sampling can sometimes provide a benefit at higher temperatures
claims.modelEra: June 2025 assessment of the min-p evidence base across Qwen, Mistral, Llama and Gemma models. THIS IS THE ANSWER TO THE ROSTER'S HIGH-TEMPERATURE CLAIM: the peer-reviewed 'high temperature can be made coherent' result survives only as a weak effect inside a regime that is worse overall.

claims.claim: Paech and colleagues measured that some over-used patterns appear over one thousand times more often in language-model output than in human text.
claims.source: Samuel J Paech, Allen G Roush, Judah Goldfeder and Ravid Shwartz-Ziv, 'Antislop: A Comprehensive Framework for Identifying and Eliminating Repetitive Patterns in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 21 Oct 2025
claims.quote: slop patterns appear over 1,000× more frequently in LLM output
claims.modelEra: Gemma-3-12B, Mistral-Small-3.2 and Llama-3.3-70B, 2,000 generations per model from Reddit creative-writing prompts, October 2025; human baseline: wordfreq plus a curated corpus of Reddit creative writing and Project Gutenberg; register measured: prompted short fiction, not archival or encyclopedic.

claims.claim: Paech and colleagues measured that the name Elara appears 85,513 times more often in gemma-3-12b's creative writing than in their human baseline.
